# University of Chicago
The University of Chicago, founded in 1890 with significant support from John D. Rockefeller, is a prestigious private research university known for its rigorous academics and influential research. It offers comprehensive undergraduate and graduate programs divided into four main divisions aligned with the sciences and humanities, alongside seven professional schools including top-ranked law and business schools. The university pioneered educational innovations such as the liberal arts core curriculum and the Socratic method and continues to maintain a rich tradition of multidisciplinary research, managing national labs like Argonne and Fermilab.
Governed by a board of trustees and led by President Paul Alivisatos (since 2021), the university has an endowment valued at about $10.1 billion in 2024. Its main Hyde Park campus spans 217 acres and features a mix of Gothic and modern architecture. The university enrolls around 7,569 undergraduates and 10,968 graduate students, maintaining need-blind admissions for domestic applicants and an extremely selective acceptance rate (4.7% for recent classes). Student life includes more than 400 recognized organizations, a robust house system for undergraduates, varsity athletics competing in NCAA Division III, and unique traditions such as the annual Scavenger Hunt and Latke-Hamantash Debate. UChicago counts 101 Nobel laureates among its affiliates and notable faculty past and present, including former U.S. President Barack Obama.
